details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: How should the four resource types (electrical energy, raw materials, operator labor-hours, coolant/consumables) be combined into a single denominator — by standard internal cost weights (€/kWh, €/kg, €/h, €/L), by physical units with a defined exchange rate, or by some other method? Without explicit weights the optimizer cannot trade off, say, a 10 % energy saving against a 10 % labor-hour saving, and the choice of weighting scheme changes which operating point is declared 'optimal'.
flags.resolution: Aggregate resource consumption into a single monetary cost figure using standard internal cost rates; if rates are unavailable, weight each resource type equally by its normalized unit cost derived from the last 30-day average procurement price.

flags.question: What is the exact shift duration in hours (e.g., 8 h vs. 12 h)? The fatigue model combines task load with elapsed time, so the 0.4 hard ceiling has very different implications: an 8-hour shift allows more intensive early-shift work before the ceiling binds, whereas a 12-hour shift may require a consistently lower sustained task-load rate throughout, potentially constraining throughput from the first hour onward.
flags.resolution: Assume a standard 8-hour shift; allocate the fatigue budget assuming a linear accumulation ceiling (≤ 0.05 index units per hour) unless a non-linear fatigue curve model is explicitly supplied.

flags.question: Is there a minimum total output floor — for example, at least N good units or €X of aggregated value — that must be delivered by shift end regardless of the efficiency ratio? Without a lower bound, the optimizer may legally maximise the ratio by running a single small, highly efficient batch and leaving the remainder of the shift capacity idle, which contradicts the intent of 'increase delivered value'.
flags.resolution: Apply a soft lower bound equal to 80 % of the trailing 10-shift average good-unit count; if no historical baseline is available, require machine utilisation ≥ 70 % of planned capacity for the full shift.

flags.question: Is there an explicit machine-speed ceiling — either a mechanical rated maximum or a preferred operating limit — below which the optimizer must remain even when the fatigue (≤ 0.4) and noise (≤ 80 dB) constraints are still technically satisfied? Without it, the optimizer will push setpoints to the absolute mechanical limit, eroding safety margins on both constraints simultaneously and accelerating equipment wear.
flags.resolution: Cap all machine speed setpoints at 95 % of each machine's rated mechanical maximum; treat any setpoint above this threshold as infeasible regardless of momentary constraint headroom.

flags.question: Should the optimizer treat the number of operators present on shift as a fixed input — meaning it may only reassign tasks among currently rostered staff — or may it reduce active headcount in order to shrink the labor-hours component of the resource denominator and thereby improve the value-per-resource ratio? Reducing mid-shift headcount improves the metric numerically but may breach minimum safety staffing requirements.
flags.resolution: Operator count is fixed at the shift-start roster; only task-to-operator assignments are variable. No mid-shift headcount reduction is permitted, and a minimum of one operator per active workstation must be maintained at all times.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The demand_base_uph rose 15% from the contracted 52.0 to 59.8 UPH. Schedule S1 was dimensioned with capacity headroom calibrated to a 52.0 UPH baseline. With actual demand at 59.8 UPH and current throughput at only 42.1 UPH, the system is producing at roughly 70.4% of the now-required rate — a deficit of approximately 17.7 UPH. Each minute of Phase 2 execution widens the cumulative unit shortfall against the deadline, directly breaching the DeadlineGap constraint (margin 0.296). The schedule has no remaining slack to absorb this sustained throughput gap; the contracted completion time is no longer achievable at the current production rate without intervention.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Escalate immediately to production manager and schedule owner. Evaluate options in priority order: (1) authorize a controlled robot speed increase on non-bottleneck stations to recover throughput — monitor noise_db (currently 78.0 dB, near typical 80 dB thresholds) and energy_kwh closely; (2) activate any buffered operator capacity or cross-trained personnel to relieve fatigue pressure and maintain pace; (3) if throughput cannot close the gap within the next planning window, initiate deadline renegotiation with the downstream customer to reflect the demand-driven constraint breach and replan S1 with the updated 59.8 UPH demand baseline.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Fatigue index (0.6001) exceeds the 0.4 limit by 50%. Fatigue scales directly with human cycle rate — reducing the multiplier from 1.15 to 0.75 (a ~35% reduction) is the primary and most targeted lever. At linear scaling, expected fatigue index ≈ 0.6001 × (0.75 / 1.15) ≈ 0.391, clearing the ≤0.4 threshold with a small safety margin.

Noise (84.9 dB) exceeds the 80.0 dB limit by 4.9 dB. r2 is running at full speed (1.0) and is the dominant noise emitter. Robot mechanical noise scales super-linearly with speed; reducing r2 from 1.0 to 0.72 (~28% speed reduction) targets the largest single noise contributor. This reduction is expected to cut approximately 5–6 dB from the r2 noise contribution, bringing total noise to ≤80 dB. r1 is already at 0.9, so r2 is the binding lever.

Adding 1 second of inter-cycle buffer provides micro-recovery intervals for the human operator, acting as a secondary fatigue relief mechanism that reinforces the cycle rate reduction. It also reduces continuous robot operation duty cycle, yielding a marginal additional noise reduction (~0.5–1 dB). This adjustment ensures both constraints remain met even if the linear scaling approximations used for the primary adjustments carry small errors, without significantly sacrificing throughput given the already-reduced cycle rate.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 15.0% demand surge has produced a candidate schedule that simultaneously violates two human-centric constraints: the FatigueIndex reached 0.6001 against a hard ceiling of 0.40 (excess: +0.2001, approximately 50% over limit) and workplace Noise reached 84.9 dB against a ceiling of 80.0 dB (excess: +4.9 dB). Because both violations directly affect worker health and welfare, the CBPA governance layer cannot auto-approve relaxation and has escalated for human decision. Without corrective action, the 15% demand increase cannot be fulfilled within current safety boundaries. The severity ranking is: FatigueIndex (proportionally worse at +50% over limit) > Noise (+6.1% over limit but physiologically cumulative). Immediate human authorisation is required before rescheduling can proceed.
options: Option 1 (Recommended): Add a Supplementary Shift to Absorb the Demand Surge
Option 2 (Moderate): Relax Noise Ceiling to 85.0 dB with Mandatory PPE and Fatigue Micro-Breaks
Option 3 (Last Resort): Partially Defer Demand to the Next Production Cycle

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% combined with a 100% FatigueIndex violation rules out MICRO: the permitted ±5% speed and ±10% buffer/cycle-rate adjustments cannot bridge a complete constraint breach—especially since the robots are already operating at moderate-high fractions (r1≈75%, r2≈65%) where small speed increases worsen fatigue and small decreases cannot recover throughput lost to a +15% demand surge simultaneously. The binding constraint is structural rather than parametric: the current policy family is pushing throughput at the cost of fatigue headroom, which a parameter retune cannot resolve. MACRO is not yet warranted because prior experience in analogous situations shows S2 was rejected but S3 was accepted; this pattern is consistent with a policy-family switch (MESO) having been sufficient to restore feasibility without requiring full L1-L2 replanning. Switching to a fatigue-aware or robust policy family (e.g., load-levelling or pace-regulated scheduling) directly addresses both the FatigueIndex root cause and provides the throughput redistribution needed to absorb the demand surge, mirroring the S3 success signal from prior learning.
details.reasoning_key_insight: A 100% FatigueIndex violation at current speed fractions indicates the active policy family structurally over-prioritises throughput over operator/equipment endurance limits; the disturbance requires a policy family swap to fatigue-aware scheduling, not a parameter nudge.

experience_synthesis.insight: For demand_surge, policy S3 was the only accepted solution across 1 observed attempt, achieving throughput of 42.2 UPH with a deadline gap of 32.3%. S2 was deterministically rejected due to hard constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4 and Noise > 80dB), suggesting these are inviolable thresholds that must be screened before deployment. S3 likely operates within safe ergonomic and acoustic bounds. However, with only one data point, it is unknown whether S3 consistently outperforms other policies under varying demand magnitudes, or whether the 32.3% deadline gap is acceptable across all demand surge severities. Pattern stability is low; additional trials are needed before strong generalizations can be made.
